Every family has a dish that tastes like home, and for us, it has always been chicken adobo. My grandmother made it in a dented pot that had seen decades of Sunday lunches, never once measuring the vinegar or soy sauce. She cooked by smell and by memory, tasting as she went, and somehow it came out the same every time.

The beauty of adobo is its simplicity. Chicken, vinegar, soy sauce, garlic, bay leaves, and black peppercorns simmer together until the meat turns tender and the sauce becomes rich, tangy, and deeply savory. The kitchen fills with a sharp, garlicky aroma that pulls everyone toward the table long before the rice is ready.

This recipe is my best attempt to put her instincts on paper. It has been passed down, argued over, and adjusted by three generations of cooks. I hope it finds a place at your table too.

In our family, the smell of vinegar and garlic simmering on the stove means one thing: someone is making Lola's chicken adobo. My grandmother learned this recipe in her mother's kitchen in Batangas, and she carried it with her across an ocean, written nowhere but in her memory. She never measured anything. A splash of soy sauce, a generous pour of vinegar, a handful of crushed garlic, a few bay leaves, and whole peppercorns went into the pot by instinct alone.

It took years of standing beside her, watching and tasting, before we finally captured her method on paper. The result is tender chicken braised in a tangy, savory sauce that begs to be spooned over steamed rice.

Every Filipino family swears their adobo is the best, and we are no exception. This dish has fed us through birthdays, homecomings, and ordinary Tuesday nights. Now we share it with you.

Sunlight looks white, but it's actually all the colors of the rainbow mixed together. You can see this when light passes through a prism, or when raindrops split it into a rainbow.

Light travels in waves, and each color has a different wavelength. Red light has long, stretched-out waves. Blue light has short, choppy ones.

When sunlight enters Earth's atmosphere, it crashes into tiny gas molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules are much smaller than the light waves themselves, and they scatter short waves far more strongly than long ones. So red and orange light mostly zoom straight through, while blue light gets bounced around in every direction, like a pinball. This is called Rayleigh scattering.

Because blue light is bouncing all over the sky, it reaches your eyes from every direction. That's why the whole sky glows blue.

Violet light scatters even more than blue, so why isn't the sky purple? The sun gives off less violet, and our eyes aren't very sensitive to it.

Sunsets work the same way. When the sun is low, its light travels through much more air to reach you. Most of the blue gets scattered away, leaving the reds and oranges.

Sunlight looks white, but it is actually a mix of all the colors of the rainbow. Each color travels as a wave, and the waves come in different sizes. Red light has long, stretched out waves. Blue light has short, tightly packed waves.

When sunlight reaches Earth, it has to pass through our atmosphere, which is full of tiny gas molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules are far smaller than the light waves themselves. When light bumps into them, it gets bounced off in all directions. Scientists call this scattering.

Here is the key part: short waves scatter much more easily than long ones. Blue light gets scattered about ten times more than red light. So while red and orange light mostly travel straight through the air, blue light gets bounced all over the sky. No matter where you look, some of that scattered blue light is heading toward your eyes. That makes the whole sky appear blue.

You might wonder why the sky isn't violet, since violet waves are even shorter. The Sun gives off less violet light, and our eyes are not very sensitive to it.

At sunset, sunlight travels through much more air to reach you. Most of the blue gets scattered away before it arrives, leaving the reds and oranges behind.

When you visit a website, your browser downloads many files: images, fonts, stylesheets, and scripts. Downloading takes time, so your browser saves copies of these files on your device. This storage area is called the **cache**.

The next time you visit that site, your browser checks its cache first. If it already has a file, it loads the saved copy instead of downloading it again. That's why a website often loads faster on your second visit.

It's a bit like keeping groceries in your kitchen. Instead of going to the store every time you want milk, you grab it from the fridge.

But what if the website changes? Like milk, cached files have an expiration date. Websites tell your browser how long each file can be kept. Once that time is up, the browser asks the website, "Has this changed?" If not, it keeps using its copy. If so, it downloads the new version.

Occasionally the cache causes problems, such as showing an outdated version of a page. That's why tech support often suggests "clearing your cache," which deletes the saved files and forces your browser to download everything fresh.

In short, the cache trades a little storage space for faster browsing and less data use.

When you visit a website, your browser has to download everything on the page: images, fonts, style files, and scripts. Downloading takes time, so your browser saves copies of these files on your device. This storage area is called the cache.

The next time you visit that site, the browser checks the cache first. If it already has a file, it loads the saved copy instead of downloading it again. This makes pages appear much faster and uses less data.

Think of it like keeping a cookbook at home. Instead of driving to the library every time you need a recipe, you grab the copy from your own shelf.

But what if the website changes? Websites tell the browser how long each file can be trusted, such as an hour, a day, or a year. Once that time runs out, the browser asks the website whether the file has changed. If it has not, the browser keeps using its copy. If it has, the browser downloads the new version.

Sometimes the cache holds outdated files, and a page looks broken or old. That is why "clear your cache" is common troubleshooting advice. Clearing it deletes the saved copies, forcing the browser to download everything fresh.

One year ago I became an engineering manager. Here's what I got wrong, and what I learned.

**1. My job changed, and I didn't.** For months I kept grabbing tickets to feel productive. Every one I took was a growth opportunity I stole from someone else.

**2. One-on-ones aren't status updates.** The best ones barely touched the sprint board. Asking "what's frustrating you right now?" surfaced more problems than any dashboard.

**3. Delayed feedback is expensive.** I once waited three weeks to raise a hard conversation. By then it had grown from a five-minute chat into a real problem.

**4. Clarity beats cleverness.** My team didn't need my architecture opinions. They needed to know what mattered most and why.

**5. Output is the wrong scoreboard.** I now measure my weeks by what the team shipped and learned, not what I did.

I'm still learning. What do you wish you'd known in your first year as a manager?

One year ago, I traded my IDE for a calendar full of one-on-ones. Here is what my first year as an engineering manager taught me.

1. Your output is now your team's output. I had to stop measuring my worth by the code I shipped and start measuring it by how well others could ship theirs.

2. Listening beats solving. My instinct was to jump in with fixes. Most of the time, people needed space to think out loud, not my answer.

3. Clarity is kindness. Vague feedback feels gentle in the moment but helps no one. Specific feedback delivered with care builds trust.

4. Protect focus time. Every meeting I decline on my team's behalf is a gift to their productivity.

5. You will get things wrong. Own it quickly, learn, and move on.

I am still learning every day, and I am grateful to the team that made this year so rewarding.

New managers, what was your biggest lesson?

# *Frankenstein* by Mary Shelley (1818)

**Plot:** Victor Frankenstein, a brilliant and ambitious young scientist, becomes obsessed with discovering the secret of life. After months of feverish work, he animates a creature assembled from corpses, then flees in horror at what he has made. Abandoned, the Creature teaches himself language and longs for human connection, but his appearance earns him only fear and violence. Embittered, he murders Victor's young brother and demands that Victor build him a female companion. Victor begins, then destroys the unfinished mate, and the Creature retaliates by killing Victor's closest friend and his bride, Elizabeth. Victor pursues him into the Arctic, where he dies aboard an explorer's ship. The Creature, grieving over his creator's body, vanishes into the ice to end his own life.

**Themes:** Shelley's novel warns against unchecked ambition, showing how the pursuit of knowledge without foresight can bring ruin. It is equally a story about responsibility: Victor's true failure is not creating life but abandoning it. The Creature's transformation from gentle to vengeful raises the question of whether monsters are born or made by rejection and isolation. Throughout, the novel blurs the line between creator and creation, asking which of the two is truly monstrous.

**Frankenstein by Mary Shelley (1818)**

**Plot:** Victor Frankenstein, a brilliant young scientist from Geneva, becomes obsessed with uncovering the secret of life. After years of feverish study, he assembles a creature from dead body parts and brings it to life. Horrified by what he has made, he abandons it. The creature, intelligent and sensitive, wanders alone and learns language by secretly observing a family. Rejected by everyone he meets because of his appearance, he grows bitter and seeks out his creator. When Victor refuses to build him a companion, the creature takes revenge by killing those Victor loves, including his friend Henry and his bride Elizabeth. Victor pursues him into the Arctic, where he dies aboard an explorer's ship. The creature mourns him and vanishes into the ice, intending to end his own life.

**Themes:** The novel explores the dangers of unchecked ambition and the pursuit of knowledge without regard for consequences. It also asks what creators owe to what they create, since Victor's neglect, more than the creature's nature, drives the tragedy. Isolation runs throughout: both Victor and the creature suffer from loneliness, suggesting that cruelty is often born from rejection. Finally, Shelley questions who the real monster is, blurring the line between human and inhuman.

**1/** Clever code impresses for the ten minutes it takes to write. Simple code pays off for the ten years it takes to maintain. Here's why boring wins.

**2/** Code is read far more often than it's written. That one-liner with nested ternaries saved you four lines once. It costs every future reader five minutes, forever.

**3/** Kernighan's law: debugging is twice as hard as writing the code in the first place. So if you write the cleverest code you're capable of, you are by definition not smart enough to debug it.

**4/** Requirements change. Simple code is easy to modify and easy to delete. Clever abstractions bake in guesses about the future, and when those guesses turn out wrong, you have to untangle the cleverness before you can fix anything.

**5/** Simple isn't easy, though. Finding the plain solution often takes more thought than the tricky one. When you do need a trick, like in a hot loop, isolate it and comment why. Spend your cleverness on the problem, not the syntax.

**1/5**
Clever code feels great to write. Simple code feels great to read. Code gets read far more often than it gets written, so guess which one pays off. Here's why boring wins. 🧵

**2/5**
Debugging is harder than writing. Kernighan said it best: if you write code as cleverly as you possibly can, you are by definition not smart enough to debug it. Leave yourself some headroom.

**3/5**
Your code has an audience: the teammate who joined last week, the on-call engineer at 3am, and you in six months with zero memory of what you were thinking. None of them want a puzzle. They want to understand it fast and move on.

**4/5**
Simple code is cheap to change. Requirements shift, and when they do, plain logic bends while clever tricks break. That elegant one liner packed with assumptions becomes a full rewrite the moment one assumption stops being true.

**5/5**
Clever code shows off the author. Simple code serves the reader. The real skill is taking a hard problem and making the solution look obvious. Write code that makes people say "oh, that's it?" That's the compliment to aim for.

**A Toast to Daniel and Claire**

Good evening, everyone. I'm Sam, and I've known Daniel since we were six years old, back when his greatest ambition was digging a hole to China in my backyard.

Over thirty years, I've watched him grow from that muddy, stubborn kid into the most loyal person I know. He's the friend who shows up—at 2 a.m. with a spare tire, at every graduation, at every heartbreak.

But I'd never seen him truly speechless until he met Claire. He called me after their first date and just said, "I'm in trouble." He was right.

Claire, you bring out a calm and a joy in him that the rest of us spent decades trying to find. Thank you for loving my best friend so well.

Please raise your glasses. To Daniel and Claire: may your life together be full of laughter, patience, and adventures more successful than that hole ever was.
